The naive answers are wrong in opposite directions: splitting credit equally ignores that some steps did the real work, and crediting whoever produced the final text ignores everyone whose output it was built on. title: [PROPOSAL] Cookbook: Giving an agent a grounded view of its own behavior over time
author: WGlynn
body_preview: An agent usually has no view of its own behavior over time. Each turn starts fresh, so a slow drift (more retries, more tool errors, longer paths to the same result) is invisible to it even though the signal is sitting in its own logs. A small self-observation step closes that gap: the agent periodically reads its own recent activity and produces a short report on how it is doing, including flags...

title: [PROPOSAL] Cookbook: Pipeline vs barrier — composing sub-agents without wasting parallelism
author: WGlynn
body_preview: When a task splits into independent parts, running them through one agent in sequence wastes most of the available parallelism, and forcing every part to finish before any downstream work starts wastes more. title: [PROPOSAL] Cookbook: Reconciling an agent's outputs across contexts before they ship
author: WGlynn
body_preview: An agent that works across several separate contexts, sessions, or sub-agents can end up contradicting itself: a decision made in one place is unknown to another, and the two outputs disagree. The contradiction is usually invisible at the moment it is produced, because each context looks internally consistent.  The pattern that helps is a reconciliation pass before a result is treated as final. In...

author: WGlynn
body_preview: Most agent safety lives inside the prompt: the model is told what not to do and usually complies. Usually is the problem. A more robust place to put an invariant is outside the model, as a check that runs on every tool call regardless of what the model intended, and can block or rewrite the call before it takes effect. A more interesting loop is one where the agent improves its own tooling between runs: it does the task, notices where it was slow or where it had to redo work, edits the small script or prompt it used, and the next run is faster or cleaner because of that edit. title: [PROPOSAL] Cookbook: A symbolic operator notation for compact agent state
author: WGlynn
body_preview: A long-running agent spends a lot of its context on its own notes, plans, and memory, written in ordinary prose. Prose is redundant: articles, connectives, and hedging words carry little of the meaning but most of the bytes. If the agent instead writes that internal state in a compact symbolic notation, the same content takes far less room, and in my experience the model reads it back just as well...

In practice free prose drifts: the agent paraphrases its earlier note, softens a hard rule, or quietly drops a constraint. The failure is silent, which is the worst kind.
